text:
Predicates:
ScheduleMeeting(x, y) ::: x schedules a meeting with y.
AppearInCompany(x) ::: x appears in the company today.
HasLunchInCompany(x) ::: x has lunch in the company.
HasLunchAtHome(x) ::: x has lunch at home.
WorkRemotelyFromHome(x) ::: x works remotely from home.
Manager(x) ::: x is a manager.
InOtherCountries(x) ::: x is in other countries.
Employee(x) ::: x is an employee.
Premises:
∀x (Employee(x) ∧ ScheduleMeeting(x, customers) → AppearInCompany(x)) ::: All employees who schedule a meeting with their customers will appear in the company today.
∀x (HasLunchInCompany(x) → ScheduleMeeting(x, customers)) ::: Everyone who has lunch in the company schedules meetings with their customers.
∀x (Employee(x) → (HasLunchInCompany(x) ∨ HasLunchAtHome(x))) ::: Employees will either have lunch in the company or have lunch at home.
∀x (HasLunchAtHome(x) → WorkRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: If an employee has lunch at home, then he/she is working remotely from home.
∀x (Employee(x) ∧ InOtherCountries(x) → WorkRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: All employees who are in other countries work remotely from home.
∀x (Manager(x) → ¬WorkRemotelyFromHome(x)) ::: No managers work remotely from home.
(Manager(james) ∧ AppearInCompany(james)) ⊕ ¬(Manager(james) ∨ AppearInCompany(james)) ::: James is either a manager and appears in the company today or neither a manager nor appears in the company today.
Conclusion:
¬HasLunchInCompany(james) ::: James does not have lunch in the company.
